title: Gold Is a Pet Rock
text:
by Craig Hemke, Sprott Money:
Why Gold Is a Store of Value
Eleven years ago this week, the Wall Street Journal published an essay entitled, “Let’s Be Honest About Gold: It’s A Pet Rock”, unwittingly marking the bottom of a brutal, two-year bear market. And, to their point, let’s be honest about it. Gold really is a pet rock…just not for the reasons listed in the article.
Let’s start with a link to the post from July 17, 2015. It’s behind a paywall now, but if you have a Wall Street Journal subscription, you can read it here.
TRUTH LIVES on at https://sgtreport.tv/
To save you time, here are the first two paragraphs, and if you swap out some of the old headlines for current headlines, it reads like it was written last week. Gold is “not a safe haven”, “it’s down 39% from its peak”, and as such, “investors are yanking billions out of gold funds”.
Wall Street Journal “Let’s Be Honest About Gold: It’s a Pet Rock” Article (July 2015)
Gold vs Fiat Currency
I’ll save you the old “history not repeating but rhyming” stuff and focus instead upon what Jason Zweig inadvertently got right, that whole “pet rock” thing.
You see, gold really is a pet rock, or pet metal, whichever you prefer. It truly does just sit there and collect dust as it pays no interest or dividends and has no utility. But that’s the point! Its value is not measurable. It IS the measure.
The investment world expresses value in fiat currency…think dollars per share or dollars per ounce. But in doing this, the miscalculation is that the dollar is the measuring stick. As if the dollar has the stable underlying value. However, we all know that’s untrue. The dollar, or any other fiat currency for that matter, is constantly being devalued by new issuance. The supply of dollars continues to grow, thereby devaluing and diluting the dollars that were already in circulation.
U.S. M2 Money Supply Growth Chart (2000–2026)
Learn more about live precious metals pricing.
Gold Price and Money Supply
Of course, some will claim that gold gets diluted 1% per year via new mine supply, but that’s nothing compared to the long-term growth of M2 money supply, which averages 6-7% per year.
